topics.summary: Why the interface may only be touched from one thread, how to send slow work elsewhere, and the mistakes that freeze the app or corrupt the data.

lesson.heading: One thread for the interface
lesson.body:
A **thread** is a line of work the processor follows. An app has several, but one of them is special: the **main thread**. It is the one that draws the interface, receives taps and keeps the screen alive.

There is one rule, and it is absolute: **everything to do with UIKit happens on the main thread.** Setting a label's text, adding a view, pushing a screen.

The reason is not arbitrary. UIKit is not built to be touched by two threads at once; it has no locks, deliberately, because locking everything would make it slower for everybody. And the drawing happens on the main thread's run loop, so a change made somewhere else may be seen halfway through.

The symptoms when you break it are nasty precisely because they are not consistent: a label that does not update, a view that appears in the wrong place, a crash once a week with a stack trace that makes no sense. Xcode can catch it for you — the Main Thread Checker is on by default and prints a warning the moment you do it.

The other half of the rule: **slow work must not be on the main thread.** While it is busy, nothing is drawn and nothing responds. A third of a second is noticeable; two seconds and the user thinks the app has died.

So: slow work elsewhere, result back to the main thread. Every network callback is written this way.

lesson.heading: Queues: async, sync, serial, concurrent
lesson.body:
You do not create threads by hand. You put work on a **queue**, and the system decides which thread runs it. The tool is **GCD**, and four words cover nearly everything.

**`async`** — hand the work over and carry on immediately. This is what you want nearly always.
**`sync`** — hand it over and **wait** here until it is finished. Dangerous.
**Serial** — one job at a time, in order. Safe: two jobs can never touch the same data at once.
**Concurrent** — several at once. Fast, and unsafe if they share anything.

The mistake that freezes the app completely: **`DispatchQueue.main.sync` called from the main thread**. You are saying "wait here until the main queue has run this" — but the main queue is the one you are standing on, and it cannot run anything until you let go. Both wait forever. It is not a slowdown, it is a dead app.

The other thing worth knowing is **QoS**, the priority: `.userInteractive` for something the user is watching happen, `.userInitiated` for something they just asked for, `.utility` for a progress bar, `.background` for a backup. Picking a lower one is not just politeness: it saves battery and lets the system do the urgent things first.

lesson.heading: Waiting for several things at once
lesson.body:
You often have to start three downloads and do something when all three are done. **`DispatchGroup`** counts for you: `enter()` before each job, `leave()` when it finishes, and `notify` runs once the count is back to zero.

The rule is unforgiving and is the classic bug: **every `enter` needs exactly one `leave`, on every path out, including the failure one.** Miss a `leave` and the count never reaches zero, so `notify` is never called and the screen waits forever. Call `leave` twice and the app stops with a crash.

The defence is `defer`, which runs whichever way you leave. Put `defer { group.leave() }` as the first line of the closure and you cannot forget it.

The other trap in the same code: the results usually get appended to a shared array from several queues at once. That is a **race**, and it corrupts the array. Append on a serial queue, or on the main one.

**`OperationQueue`** sits one level up. It costs a little more, and it gives you three things GCD does not: dependencies between jobs, cancellation, and a limit on how many run at once.

lesson.heading: Races: when two threads touch one thing
lesson.body:
A **race condition** is two pieces of code touching the same data at the same time, with at least one of them writing.

The thing to understand is why even `count += 1` is unsafe. That one line is really three steps: read the value, add one, write it back. Two threads can both read 5, both work out 6, and both write 6. Two increments, one result. Nothing crashes, the number is just quietly wrong.

That is what makes races the worst kind of bug: there is no error, no crash, just a value that is occasionally not what it should be, on one device, once in a thousand runs.

The defences, from oldest to newest:

**A serial queue.** Everything that touches the data goes through one queue. Simple and effective.
**A concurrent queue with a barrier.** Many readers at once, one writer alone. Good for a cache that is read far more than written.
**An actor.** The modern answer: a type that guarantees one at a time, and the compiler enforces it instead of you remembering.

To find them, Xcode has the **Thread Sanitizer**: switch it on in the scheme and it reports races as they happen, with both stack traces. It is slow, which is why it is a thing you turn on deliberately.

lesson.heading: Where modern async code actually runs
lesson.body:
With `async/await` the question changes shape, and the answer surprises people.

**`Task { }` inherits the context it was created in.** Started from a `@MainActor` class — and a `UIViewController` is one — the whole body runs on the main thread. So a slow synchronous function called inside it blocks the interface exactly as before. The `Task` did not move anything anywhere.

To actually get off the main thread you need something that is not isolated to it: a method on an `actor`, a function marked `nonisolated`, or `Task.detached` as a last resort.

**`await` does not block.** At that point the function is put aside and the thread is freed. That is why `await` on the main thread is fine — the interface keeps running — while `DispatchQueue.main.sync` is fatal.

**`@MainActor` replaces the manual hop.** Marking the view model means the compiler checks for you, at build time, that the interface is only touched from the right place — instead of you finding out at runtime, once a week.

questions.prompt: Which thread does a `URLSession.shared.dataTask` completion run on?
options: A background queue: to touch the interface you have to hop back
questions.explanation: The callback arrives on one of the session's own background queues. Touching the interface from there breaks the main thread rule, which is why every network callback ends with a `DispatchQueue.main.async` or an `await MainActor.run`.
whyWrong: If it were, there would be no need for the `main.async` you see in every example.
Which thread called `resume` makes no difference: the callback comes from the session's own queues.
The priority is not fixed, and in any case it is never the main thread.

questions.prompt: What happens when this runs on the main thread?
options: It freezes for good: the system notices and the app dies
The block runs on the next run loop pass
questions.explanation: `sync` means "wait here until the main queue has run this". But the main queue is the one you are standing on, and it cannot start anything until you let go. Each waits for the other, forever. The system detects it and stops the app.
whyWrong: For it to run immediately the queue would have to be free. It is not: you are occupying it.
Deferring to the next pass is what `async` does, and that version is perfectly safe here.
Nothing converts it. `sync` means `sync`, which is exactly the problem.

questions.prompt: What does this print, running on the main thread?
questions.explanation: `async` puts the block in the queue and carries straight on. The main queue is busy running this very function, so the block waits its turn: it only runs once the current work is finished. Hence 1, 3, and then 2.
whyWrong: That is what `sync` would give — except `sync` here would freeze the app instead.
Nothing runs before line 1: `async` does not jump the queue.
There is nothing unpredictable: the main queue is serial, so the order is always the same.

questions.prompt: Here `notify` is sometimes never called. Why?
options: `enter` has to be inside the closure
Groups do not work with closures
questions.explanation: The `guard` leaves without calling `leave`, so on a failure the count never comes back down and `notify` waits forever. The fix is `defer { group.leave() }` as the first line, which runs on every way out.
whyWrong: `enter` has to be before the job starts, which is exactly where it is.
`notify` is registered whenever you like: it fires when the count reaches zero.
They work with closures perfectly well. The problem is the missing `leave`.

questions.prompt: What does `.barrier` do on `DispatchQueue.global()`?
options: Nothing: it behaves like a normal `async`
It blocks all the global queues
It only serialises work with the same priority
questions.explanation: A barrier only works on a concurrent queue you created yourself, because it has to be able to hold everything else back. The global queues are shared by the whole system, so the flag is ignored — silently, which is why the bug is hard to spot.
whyWrong: Blocking shared queues would be unthinkable: other parts of the app and the system use them.
Priority has nothing to do with it. The flag is simply ignored.
Nothing stops. It is quietly ineffective, which is worse than an error.

questions.prompt: Why must UIKit be used only from the main thread?
options: The main thread has more memory
UIKit is not built for two threads at once, and drawing happens on its run loop
questions.explanation: UIKit has no internal locking, deliberately: locking everything would make it slower for everyone. And the drawing happens on the main run loop, so a change made elsewhere can be picked up halfway through. The result is unpredictable, which is the worst kind of bug.
whyWrong: Memory is shared by every thread: it has nothing to do with it.
They can create them — that is exactly the problem: nothing stops you, and then it misbehaves.
It is just as true on a device. The simulator only has more checks switched on.

questions.prompt: What does `OperationQueue` give you that plain GCD does not?
options: It runs on the main thread by default
Dependencies between jobs, cancellation, and a limit on how many run at once
questions.explanation: Those three are the reason to pay the slightly higher cost. "Resize only after the download finishes", "cancel what is in flight when the screen closes", "never more than three at a time" are all one line each.
whyWrong: It is slightly slower: it is built on top of GCD and adds its own bookkeeping.
It runs wherever you tell it. `OperationQueue.main` is the one that is on the main thread.
It prevents nothing by itself: shared data still has to be protected.

questions.prompt: What does this print?
questions.code:
var count = 0
DispatchQueue.concurrentPerform(iterations: 1000) { _ in
    count += 1
}
print(count)
options: It does not build in Swift 5
An unpredictable number, usually less than 1000
questions.explanation: `+= 1` is three steps: read, add, write. Several threads read the same value, work out the same result, and write it. Increments get lost, and the number is different every run. This is a race, and nothing warns you about it.
whyWrong: 1000 would require each increment to be indivisible. It is not.
Something does get counted: it is just less than it should be.
It builds. Swift 5 does not check this, which is why Swift 6 tightened the rules.

questions.prompt: What defines a serial queue?
options: It always runs on the main thread
It runs jobs in parallel but in order
It runs one job at a time, in the order they arrived
It uses one fixed thread for the whole life of the app
questions.explanation: One at a time, first in first out. That is what makes it safe for shared data: while one job is running, no other can be touching the same thing.
whyWrong: The main queue is serial, but not every serial queue is the main one. You create your own.
"In parallel but in order" is a contradiction: parallel means at the same time.
The system may use different threads for different jobs. What it guarantees is the order, not the thread.

questions.prompt: Which thread does `heavyParse()` run on here, inside a view controller?
options: The main thread: the Task inherits the controller's isolation
A background thread from the pool
A new thread made just for it
questions.explanation: `Task { }` inherits where it was created, and a `UIViewController` is `@MainActor`. So the body runs on the main thread, and a slow synchronous function inside it freezes the interface exactly as before. A `Task` is not a way to get off the main thread.
whyWrong: That is what `Task.detached` or an actor's method would give you. A plain `Task` inherits.
Nothing creates a thread here: the body is simply queued on the main actor.
It does not depend on anything: the rule is fixed and the result is always the same.

topics.title: Organising the code
topics.summary: MVC, MVVM, VIPER and coordinators — what problem each one actually solves, and how objects should talk to each other.

lesson.heading: MVC, and why it goes wrong
lesson.body:
The pattern Apple shipped UIKit with is **MVC**: Model, View, Controller. The model holds the data, the view shows it, the controller sits in between.

On paper the controller is a thin layer of glue. In practice, everything with nowhere else to go ends up in it: the network call, the date formatting, the table's data source, the navigation, the validation, the analytics. After six months a screen is two thousand lines long, and the joke writes itself: **Massive View Controller**.

The cost is not aesthetic. A file that long is one nobody can read in one sitting, two people cannot edit without conflicting, and nothing in it can be tested — because every piece of logic is tangled up with a view controller that needs a whole running app to exist.

The root of the trouble is that `UIViewController` **is** part of the view: it owns the views, follows their lifecycle, and cannot be created without UIKit. Logic put inside it inherits all of that.

So every architecture that came afterwards is answering one question: **where does the logic go, so that it is not inside the view controller?**

lesson.heading: MVVM: a layer that knows nothing about the screen
lesson.body:
**MVVM** adds one object between the model and the view: the **ViewModel**. Its job is to take the raw data and turn it into **exactly what the screen has to show**, already formatted and ready.

The one rule that makes it work: **the ViewModel must not import UIKit.** No views, no view controller, no constraints. It hands out text, numbers and booleans, and it does not care who draws them.

That single rule buys you two things. It can be tested with no screen at all — create it, call `load()`, check what it exposes. And the same ViewModel can serve a UIKit screen and a SwiftUI one without changing.

The view controller shrinks to what it is good at: it watches the ViewModel, puts the values into labels, and passes the user's actions back.

The traps worth naming: a ViewModel that reaches into the view defeats the whole thing, so does one that imports UIKit for "just a `UIColor`". And it must never hold the view controller — that way round is a retain cycle.

lesson.heading: VIPER and Clean: one box per job
lesson.body:
**VIPER** splits the screen into five objects, each with one job:

**View** — shows what it is given and reports taps. It decides nothing.
**Interactor** — the business rules and the data. No UIKit.
**Presenter** — takes what the Interactor produces, formats it, hands it to the View.
**Entity** — the plain data types.
**Router** — decides which screen comes next.

It comes from **Clean Architecture**, whose one real idea is worth knowing even if you never write a line of VIPER: **dependencies point inwards**. The rules at the centre know nothing about the database or the screen; the outside knows about the centre. So you can swap the database or the interface without touching the rules.

The honest assessment: VIPER produces five files and a protocol for each screen, and on a settings page with two switches that is pure overhead. It earns its keep in a large codebase with many people and complicated rules — banking, medical — where "where does this go?" having one obvious answer is worth more than the extra files.

For most apps, MVVM plus a coordinator gets most of the benefit at a fraction of the cost.

lesson.heading: How objects should talk to each other
lesson.body:
Whatever the architecture, objects have to pass messages. Four mechanisms, and picking the wrong one is where most mess comes from.

**Closure.** One or two things to report, one listener. Shortest and most readable. Beware the retain cycle: `[weak self]`.

**Delegate.** Several related events, one listener, and the possibility of asking a question and getting an answer back ("should I allow this?"). The protocol goes `: AnyObject` and the property goes `weak`.

**Observation.** Somebody wants to know every time a value changes. Combine with `@Published`, or the newer `@Observable`. The subscription has to be **stored**, or it is cancelled the moment it is created — a single line that silently breaks everything.

**NotificationCenter.** Several unrelated listeners, and the sender does not know who they are. Right for "the user logged out". Wrong for everything else, because it makes the flow of the app invisible: nothing in the code says who receives what.

The practical ordering: closure if one listener, delegate if several related events or an answer is needed, observation if it is about a value changing, notifications only when there are genuinely several unknown listeners.

lesson.heading: The retain cycle every architecture can hit
lesson.body:
Whatever the shape of your layers, there is one shape of bug they all share: a strong link that goes both ways.

Three places it hides:

**A back-reference.** The ViewModel or Presenter holding the view controller strongly, while the controller holds it too. The rule is simple: the thing underneath never holds the thing above strongly. `weak`.

**A notification with a closure.** `addObserver(forName:object:queue:using:)` hands its result to the centre, which holds the closure, which captures `self`. Even with the token stored, the cycle is there unless the closure is written `[weak self]`.

**An unstored subscription, or the opposite.** Not storing it means it never works; storing it in an object the subscription also captures means neither is ever freed.

The check costs nothing and catches all three: put a `print` in `deinit`, open the screen, close it. If nothing is printed, something is still holding on, and the Memory Graph Debugger will show you what.

questions.prompt: What usually makes a Massive View Controller?
options: Networking, formatting, navigation and data sources all pile into it
questions.explanation: The controller is the easiest place to put anything, so everything with nowhere else to go lands there. Two thousand lines later, nobody can read it and nothing in it can be tested, because every piece of logic needs a running app to exist.
whyWrong: A storyboard changes where the interface is described. The logic ends up in the controller either way.
Lots of subviews is a layout question, not an architecture one.
Auto Layout describes positions. It has nothing to do with how much logic is in the file.

questions.prompt: In MVVM, which of these should be true of the ViewModel?
options: It does not depend on UIKit and hands out ready-formatted state
questions.explanation: That is the whole rule, and everything good about MVVM follows from it. No UIKit means it can be tested with no screen, and it can serve a UIKit screen and a SwiftUI one without changing a line.
whyWrong: Holding the view strongly is a retain cycle waiting to happen. If it must refer back at all, that reference is `weak`.
Inheriting from a view controller would drag in UIKit and the whole view lifecycle, which is exactly what MVVM is avoiding.
Constraints are the view's business. A ViewModel that touches them is a view controller with a different name.

questions.prompt: In VIPER, which part holds the business rules?
questions.explanation: The Interactor is the centre: the rules and the data, with no UIKit anywhere. Keeping it free of the interface is what makes it testable and what lets you change the screen without touching the rules.
whyWrong: The Presenter formats and connects: it takes what the Interactor produces and makes it ready to show.
The Router only decides which screen comes next.
An Entity is a plain data type. It holds values, not rules.

questions.prompt: You need to tell several unrelated screens that the user logged out. What fits best?
questions.explanation: This is the one case notifications are genuinely right for: several listeners, the sender does not know who they are, and nobody has to be wired up. Everywhere else they are worth avoiding, because they make the flow of the app invisible.
whyWrong: A delegate is one listener. For several you would need a list, and then you have rebuilt notifications badly.
A closure is also one listener, and whoever is sending would have to know every screen.
KVO is for watching a property change, and `UIApplication` has no "logged out" property.

questions.prompt: When is a delegate better than a closure?
options: When you need one single callback
When there are several related events, or a method has to return an answer
questions.explanation: A protocol groups related events in one place and is the only one of the two that can ask a question and get an answer back — "should I allow this?". Three or four separate closure properties is where it becomes clearly worse.
whyWrong: For a single callback a closure is shorter and reads better where you create the object.
A delegate is one listener. Many listeners means notifications or observation.
"Always" is wrong: the whole of UIKit is built on delegates, and for good reasons.

questions.prompt: What do you need in order to observe a property of your own Swift class with KVO?
options: An `NSObject` subclass and an `@objc dynamic` property
questions.explanation: KVO is an Objective-C mechanism: it works by swapping the class's method at runtime, which only exists in that world. That is why it needs both the base class and the `dynamic` keyword — and why in new Swift code you use Combine or `@Observable` instead.
whyWrong: `@Published` belongs to Combine, which is a different mechanism entirely.
`Observable` is the modern Swift macro, and it has nothing to do with KVO.
Structs cannot be observed with KVO at all: there is no object and no runtime to swap anything in.

questions.prompt: What happens with this subscription in `viewDidLoad`?
options: It works for as long as the controller is alive
It crashes: the cancellable cannot be discarded
It is cancelled immediately: at most the first value arrives
questions.explanation: `sink` hands back an `AnyCancellable`, and when that is thrown away the subscription ends. The `_ =` throws it away on the spot. You have to keep it, usually with `.store(in: &cancellables)`. This is a one-line bug that produces a screen that updates once and then stops.
whyWrong: It would, if the cancellable were stored. Thrown away, it ends at once.
Nothing crashes: the result of `sink` can be discarded, which is exactly what makes the bug quiet.
The first value usually does arrive, because `@Published` sends the current one immediately. That is what makes it look like it works.

questions.prompt: In MVVM with coordinators, who decides to show the detail screen after a row is tapped?
options: The ViewModel, by pushing onto the navigation controller
The cell, through the responder chain
The coordinator, told by the ViewModel or the controller
questions.explanation: That is the point of having a coordinator: navigation is its only job. The ViewModel says "the user picked this one" and stops there, which keeps it free of UIKit and lets the same screen be used in a different flow without changing.
whyWrong: If the ViewModel touched the navigation controller it would need UIKit, and the whole benefit is gone.
A cell knows nothing about flows: its job is to show a row.
A model holds data. Deciding which screen comes next is not a data question.

questions.prompt: In Apple's MVC, why is the view controller hard to test?
options: It is tied to the view and its lifecycle
It can only be created from a storyboard
questions.explanation: To test logic inside a controller you have to create the controller, and that drags in the view, the lifecycle and a running UIKit. Pulling the logic out into an object with no UIKit — a ViewModel, an Interactor — is what makes it testable in milliseconds.
whyWrong: It can have as many dependencies as you like. The problem is everything else that comes with it.
It can contain logic — that is exactly the problem, not a restriction.
It can be created in code too. Even then, the view and its lifecycle come along.

questions.prompt: This controller is never freed. Why?
options: The centre holds the closure, and the closure holds `self` strongly
`token` is strong and makes a cycle with the centre
questions.explanation: The notification centre keeps the closure alive, and the closure captures `self` strongly, so the controller can never be freed. `[weak self]` breaks it. Storing the token and removing the observer is good practice too, but it is not what causes this leak.
whyWrong: The queue only says where the block runs. It holds nothing.
The token is a receipt, not a reference back to your controller. On its own it creates no cycle.
`@objc` is only needed for the old selector-based form, and it has nothing to do with memory.

topics.title: Memory and smoothness
topics.summary: What keeps a screen alive after you leave it, why images cost far more than their file size, and how to find the thing that makes scrolling stutter.

lesson.heading: Who is still holding the screen
lesson.body:
Swift frees an object when nobody is holding it any more: it counts the holders, and at zero the memory goes back. A **retain cycle** happens when two objects hold each other, so the count never gets to zero and neither is ever freed.

In an app with screens, this usually means a whole screen — with its views, its images, its data — stays in memory after the user has left it. Do it a few times and the app is using hundreds of megabytes for screens nobody can see.

The four places it hides, in order of how often:

**A delegate held strongly.** The rule is: a child never holds its parent strongly. `weak var delegate`, and the protocol declared `: AnyObject` so that is allowed.

**A closure stored in a property.** The object holds the closure, the closure mentions `self`. `[weak self]`.

**A repeating `Timer`.** Covered below, because `[weak self]` does not fix it.

**An observer or subscription never released.** A notification with a closure, a Combine `AnyCancellable`, a KVO token.

The check costs one line: a `print` in `deinit`. Open the screen, close it, and if nothing appears, something is holding on.

lesson.heading: Timers, and when [weak self] is not enough
lesson.body:
A repeating `Timer` is the leak that survives the usual fix, and that is why it gets asked.

The cycle is not between your closure and your controller. It is that **the run loop holds the timer**. So even with `[weak self]`, the timer stays alive and keeps firing — on a `self` that is now `nil`, doing nothing, forever, waking the processor once a second for no reason.

It has to be stopped explicitly: `invalidate()`. The right place is usually `viewWillDisappear`, or `deinit` if the controller is going to be freed at all.

With the old selector form it is worse: `scheduledTimer(timeInterval:target:selector:...)` holds its target **strongly**, so the controller is never freed, so `deinit` never runs, so the `invalidate()` you put in `deinit` never happens. A perfect loop. Either use the closure form with `[weak self]`, or stop it somewhere that definitely runs.

The modern alternative avoids the whole thing: a `Task` with a sleep inside, cancelled when the screen goes.

And while we are here: **`UIView.animate` does not need `[weak self]`**. The closure is held by the animation, which lets go when it finishes. It delays the free by a third of a second; it does not prevent it.

lesson.heading: Images: the hidden cost
lesson.body:
The biggest memory surprise in an iOS app is almost always images, and the reason is that **a file's size has nothing to do with the memory it takes**.

A JPEG is compressed. To draw it, the system has to decompress it into raw pixels, and from then on it occupies **width × height × 4 bytes** — four bytes per pixel, one for each of red, green, blue and transparency.

A photo of 4000 by 3000 is twelve million pixels, which is **48 MB** in memory. The file on disk was two. Showing twenty of them in a list is a gigabyte, and iOS will kill the app long before that.

And the thumbnail is the trap: shrinking a `UIImageView` changes nothing. The whole image is still decompressed at full size; it is only drawn smaller.

The answer is to **decompress it at the size you need**, which is what `prepareThumbnail(of:)` does — or `ImageIO` with `kCGImageSourceThumbnailMaxPixelSize`, which never has the full-size version in memory at any point.

The arithmetic worth remembering: pixels × 4. It explains a surprising number of memory problems at a glance.

lesson.heading: Why scrolling stutters
lesson.body:
The screen is redrawn sixty times a second, which leaves about sixteen milliseconds per frame. Anything that takes longer means a frame is missed, and a missed frame is a visible jerk.

The usual causes, in order of how often:

**Work on the main thread while scrolling.** Decoding an image, formatting a date, a calculation inside `cellForRowAt`. Do it elsewhere, or earlier.

**A shadow without a path.** `shadowOpacity` alone makes the system work out the shape of the shadow from the view's contents, every frame. Giving it `shadowPath` turns a calculation into a lookup, and it is the single biggest win in a list of cards.

**Rounded corners with clipping.** `cornerRadius` plus `masksToBounds` forces the view to be drawn into a separate buffer first and then composited. On one view it is nothing; on fifty cells it is visible.

**Transparency.** A view with `isOpaque = false` forces the system to blend what is behind it. If the view is in fact solid, say so.

To find out which one it is, there is **Instruments**, and the tool depends on the question: **Time Profiler** for "what is the main thread doing", **Allocations** for "what is eating the memory", **Leaks** for "what is never freed". And the Debug Navigator in Xcode shows memory and processor use live, for free, with no setup at all.
lesson.code:
// The biggest single win in a list of cards
card.layer.shadowOpacity = 0.2
card.layer.shadowRadius = 8
card.layer.shadowPath = UIBezierPath(
    roundedRect: card.bounds, cornerRadius: 12).cgPath   // not recalculated each frame

// Say so when a view really is solid
label.isOpaque = true
label.backgroundColor = .systemBackground   // not clear

// Rounded corners without forcing a separate buffer
card.layer.cornerRadius = 12
card.layer.cornerCurve = .continuous
card.clipsToBounds = false                  // and clip the image itself instead

lesson.heading: The geometry questions that keep coming up
lesson.body:
Two things get asked at this level more than anything else, so they are worth having straight.

**`frame` against `bounds`.** `frame` is the view seen from outside: where it is in its parent's coordinates. `bounds` is the view seen from inside: its own coordinate system, with the origin normally at zero.

They part company in two cases. With a `transform`, `bounds` is unchanged — inside, the view is the same rectangle — while `frame` becomes the smallest upright box that encloses the rotated view, which is bigger. And in a scroll view, scrolling moves `bounds.origin`, which is exactly what `contentOffset` is, while `frame` does not move at all.

The practical consequence: **never set `frame` on a view that has a transform.** Use `bounds` and `center` instead.

**`UIView` against `CALayer`.** Every view owns a layer, and the layer does the drawing. The view adds what a layer knows nothing about: receiving touches, taking part in Auto Layout, being in the responder chain. That is why corners, shadows and borders are all set on `view.layer`.

And one more detail: a layer does not do Auto Layout. If you add a gradient layer, you have to resize it yourself in `viewDidLayoutSubviews`, or it stays the size it was when it was created.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between `frame` and `bounds`?
options: `frame` is in the parent's coordinates, `bounds` in the view's own
`frame` includes the transform, `bounds` the safe area
questions.explanation: `frame` is the view seen from outside: where it is for its parent. `bounds` is the view seen from inside: its own coordinates, where it starts at zero. They are the same size until there is a transform or a scroll.
whyWrong: They match in the simple case, which is exactly why the difference catches people out when it appears.
Neither is in window coordinates. For that you convert explicitly, with `convert(_:to:)`.
It is the other way round: `frame` is affected by the transform. The safe area is a different thing again.

questions.prompt: What does this print?
questions.explanation: Inside, nothing happened: `bounds` is still 100 by 100. Outside, the square is tilted, and `frame` has to be an upright rectangle, so it becomes the smallest one that encloses it — 100 times the square root of two, about 141.
whyWrong: `frame` does change: that is the whole point of the question.
They are the wrong way round: it is `bounds` that stays put.
`bounds.size` is never zero: the view has a size.

questions.prompt: Why are `delegate` properties usually `weak`?
options: To stop the two objects holding each other forever
Because protocols do not support strong references
questions.explanation: The parent holds the child, and the child needs to reach the parent. If both links were strong the count would never reach zero and the whole screen would leak. `weak` on the way back breaks it.
whyWrong: There is no difference in speed. It is purely about memory.
Protocols support strong references perfectly well. The choice is deliberate.
`weak` has nothing to do with threads: a weak reference is not thread-safe by itself.

questions.prompt: After this controller is popped, `deinit` never runs. Why?
options: `#selector` creates a cycle with the class
The timer holds `self`, and the run loop holds the timer
The navigation controller holds the controller
questions.explanation: That form of `Timer` holds its target strongly, and the run loop holds the timer. So the controller can never be freed, so `deinit` never runs, so the `invalidate` inside it never happens. A perfect loop. Stop it in `viewWillDisappear`, or use the closure form with `[weak self]`.
whyWrong: A selector is just a method name. It holds nothing on its own.
The navigation controller lets go when the screen is popped: that is what popping means.
`userInfo` is extra data carried along. It has nothing to do with memory.

questions.prompt: Do you need `[weak self]` in this closure?
options: Yes, or the controller is never freed
No: nothing of yours holds the closure, so there is no cycle
No, because animations always capture weakly
questions.explanation: The closure is held by the animation system, which releases it once the animation finishes. `self` does not hold the animation, so the loop never closes. It delays the free by a third of a second, which is not a leak. Adding `[weak self]` here only adds noise.
whyWrong: It is freed a moment later than it would otherwise be, which is not the same as never.
Escaping only means it outlives the call. A cycle needs the object to hold it back, and here it does not.
It captures strongly, like any closure. What saves you is that it is released afterwards.

questions.prompt: A shadow on many cells makes scrolling stutter. What is the most effective fix?
questions.explanation: Without a path, the system works out the shape of the shadow from the view's contents, every frame, for every cell. Giving it the shape turns that into a lookup. It is the single biggest win in a list of cards.
whyWrong: `masksToBounds` clips the contents, which would cut the shadow off entirely.
A bigger radius makes it slower, not faster: there is more to blur.
Drawing it by hand means your own code runs for every frame, which is worse.

questions.prompt: What happens when you read an `unowned` reference after the object is gone?
options: It gives you the last valid value
questions.explanation: `unowned` is a promise that the object will still be there, and there is no optional and no check. If the promise is broken, reading it is reading freed memory, and Swift stops the app deliberately rather than carrying on with rubbish. `weak` is the version that checks.
whyWrong: `nil` is `weak`. `unowned` has no optional at all.
The old value is long gone: the memory may hold something completely different by now.
It builds perfectly: the compiler takes your promise at face value.

questions.prompt: Which Instruments tool tells you what is slowing the main thread down while scrolling?
questions.explanation: It samples the stack many times a second and tells you where the time actually goes. For a stutter while scrolling, the culprit is nearly always something inside `cellForRowAt` that should not be there.
whyWrong: Leaks answers "what is never freed", which is a memory question.
Allocations answers "what is taking up the memory", also a memory question.
Network shows requests and their timing, not what the processor is busy with.

questions.prompt: A 4000 by 3000 pixel JPEG, 2 MB on disk, shown as a thumbnail. Roughly how much memory does it take?
questions.explanation: To draw it, the system decompresses it into raw pixels: width times height times 4 bytes. Twelve million pixels times four is about 48 MB. The size of the file is irrelevant, and so is the size of the view — shrinking the image view changes nothing.
whyWrong: 2 MB is the compressed file. In memory it is not compressed at all.
12 million is the number of pixels, not bytes. Each pixel needs four.
200 KB would be the thumbnail, but only if you decompressed it at that size on purpose.

questions.prompt: What is the relationship between `UIView` and `CALayer`?
options: The layer only exists if you set `cornerRadius`
Every view owns a layer that does the drawing, and acts as its delegate
The view draws, the layer handles touches
questions.explanation: The layer does the drawing. The view wraps it with what a layer knows nothing about: touches, Auto Layout, the responder chain. That is why corners, shadows and borders all live on `view.layer`.
whyWrong: They are unrelated classes: a layer draws, a view wraps a layer.
The layer is there from the moment the view is created, whatever you set.
It is exactly the other way round: the layer draws, the view handles the touches.
